title: Does 'Integration Closure' add design value beyond established systems-engineering constructs?
question: Does the proposed 'Integration Closure' concept — all components, interfaces, resources, control loops and operating conditions functioning together within their permitted ranges — add explanatory or design value beyond established systems-engineering constructs such as TRL, Integration Readiness Level, System Readiness Level, interface management, system-of-systems integration, and qualification/certification closure, and if so which observable criteria distinguish it from ordinary 'system integration'?
why_now: The document is explicitly a candidate principle, not canon, and its own evidence rule requires showing added explanatory or design value across independent domains relative to existing systems-engineering terminology before canonization. The proposed `integration-closure-candidate` tag is already meant to mark new research and product cases, so unresolved overlap with established constructs would propagate an ill-defined concept into screening decisions.
real_world_anchor: Peer-reviewed systems-engineering, readiness-level and integration-management literature: TRL, Integration Readiness Level, System Readiness Level, interface management, system-of-systems integration, and qualification/certification closure.
novelty_reason: No previous topic examines systems-engineering terminology or readiness constructs; the prior standards baseline concerns sensor metadata, provenance and messaging standards, not the governance concept in `docs/integration-closure-candidate.md`.
